newsitem.title: RWANDA: First Canadians arrive in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: First Canadians arrive in Rwanda.

text.p: Three Hercules C-130 military transport planes carrying 34 Canadians arrived in the Rwandan capital Kigali on Sunday to set up a headquarters and logistical support unit for a planned international peace force.
Major Rod Babuik said between 500-700 personnel would be based in Kigali as part of the Canadian-led U.N. multinational intervention force.
"The situation is very fluid, the movement of the refugees has had a big impact on what is happening, but we have just to carry on with our plan which is to recce out sites," he told Reuters.
Since hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees starting flooding back home from Zaire on Friday, Rwanda's government has said the force is no longer needed.

"Our position is that the force was coming to create this corridor for the refugees to come home and now they are coming home. So we don't see any need for the force to come," Rwandan presidential spokesman Joseph Bideri told Reuters.
The 15-member Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of a Canadian-led multinational force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reached refugees.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said the United States and its allies might modify the plan, but U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said such a force was still needed in troubled eastern Zaire.

"I can see the need for such a force...Don't think only of what you see on the television screens. There is a huge number of refugees that are absolutely invisible but are still very much in eastern Zaire," Chretien said in a BBC radio interview.
Thousands of impoverished refugees crossed over the border for the third day running as the human tide of showed no signs of slowing.
An estimated 250,000 Rwandan Hutus have already returned home. As many as 400,000 could still come.
